title: Hilbert's 23 problems
summary: David Hilbert asks whether all of mathematics can be mechanised — question ten becomes the seed of computability.
why: The dream of a decision procedure is the thing Turing and Gödel later prove impossible, and in failing, invent computing.

figures.label: Posed
figures.value: Paris, 8 August 1900, at the International Congress of Mathematicians

figures.label: Problem ten
figures.value: settled 1970: no such procedure exists

detail: Hilbert presented ten of the problems in his Paris lecture and published all twenty-three afterwards. Several are still open; several were settled in ways he did not expect. The tenth asked for a procedure to decide whether any polynomial equation has whole-number solutions, and the broader programme — put all of mathematics on a finite, checkable footing — was stated most sharply in 1928 as the Entscheidungsproblem: a procedure to decide any mathematical statement.

The board opens here because the machine's syllabus was written before the machine. Gödel showed in 1931 that the programme could not be completed; Turing showed in 1936 that no decision procedure exists, and had to define what a procedure is to do it. The tenth problem itself was closed in 1970 by Yuri Matiyasevich, the same way: no such procedure. The ladder of machines doing mathematics starts with the list of things they were asked to do.

title: On Computable Numbers
summary: Turing defines a universal machine and proves that Hilbert's decision problem has no solution: some questions no procedure can settle.
why: One abstraction underwrites every computer built since.
firsts: First definition of a universal computing machine

figures.label: Received
figures.value: 28 May 1936; read to the London Mathematical Society on 12 November

figures.label: In print
figures.value: 23 November and 23 December 1936, in two parts of a volume dated 1937

figures.label: Answers
figures.value: Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem, in the negative

detail: To show that no procedure can decide every mathematical statement, Turing first had to say what a procedure is. His answer is a machine with a tape, a head and a finite table of rules, modelled on a person computing with pencil and paper — and then a single machine that, given another machine's table written out on its tape, does that machine's work. 'It is possible to invent a single machine which can be used to compute any computable sequence,' the paper says, and with it a program becomes something a machine can read.

The negative result follows from the universal one. If some machine could decide, of any machine's table, whether that machine will go on printing digits for ever, a diagonal argument builds a machine that contradicts itself; so there is no such machine, and Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem — a general process for deciding whether a formula is provable — has no solution. What Turing proved undecidable is a close cousin of what textbooks now call the halting problem. Alonzo Church had reached the same answer about the Entscheidungsproblem that spring by a different route; Turing added an appendix showing the two definitions equivalent, which is why the thesis that any effective procedure is a Turing machine carries both names.

The machine stayed on paper for nine years. From 1945 Turing tried to build the universal machine in electronics, and the first stored-program computer ran in Manchester on 21 June 1948. Whether the universal machine is the stored-program idea itself or only its mathematical ancestor is still argued; that it came first is not.

The board files the paper as the fence around everything else on it: some questions no program can settle, however fast it runs. Every rung of the maths lead is a machine working inside the fence this paper drew.

title: Turing asks the question
summary: Computing Machinery and Intelligence replaces “can machines think?” with a test anyone can run.
why: Three-quarters of a century on, the imitation game is still how the public decides whether a system is intelligent.
firsts: First proposed test for machine intelligence

figures.label: Published
figures.value: Mind, October 1950

figures.label: Prediction
figures.value: by 2000, an average interrogator has no better than a 70% chance of telling machine from person after five minutes

figures.label: Objections answered
figures.value: nine

figures.label: Passed, by one measure
figures.value: 2025: GPT-4.5 taken for the human 73% of the time in a three-party test

detail: Turing opens by proposing to consider whether machines can think, and then declines to: the words are too loose, and he replaces the question with a game. An interrogator questions two hidden parties by teleprinter, one a person and one a machine, and tries to tell which is which. If the interrogator decides wrongly as often as in the parlour version of the game, played between a man and a woman, the old question has been replaced by one that can be answered.

He then works through nine objections — theological, mathematical, from consciousness and from Lady Lovelace among them — and answers each. His prediction is exact enough to check: in about fifty years, computers with a storage capacity of about 10⁹ would play so well that an average interrogator would have no more than a 70% chance of the right identification after five minutes of questioning.

The last section is the one the field caught up with: instead of programming an adult mind, build a child's and educate it, with rewards and punishments and, he thought, a random element in the learning.

The test outlived its usefulness before it was formally passed. ELIZA fooled people who wanted to be understood in 1966 without passing anything; in July 2023 Nature reported that ChatGPT had broken the Turing test and that the race was on for new ways to assess AI; and in 2025, in pre-registered three-party trials, GPT-4.5, prompted to adopt a humanlike persona, was taken for the human 73% of the time — more often than the real humans were. ELIZA, run as a baseline, managed 23%. Turing's fifty years had become seventy-five, and what passed was a learning machine of the kind his last section sketched.

title: Logic Theorist proves the textbook
summary: Newell, Simon and Shaw's program proves 38 of the first 52 theorems in chapter two of Principia Mathematica, and finds one proof neater than Russell and Whitehead's. The journal declines to list it as an author.
why: The first program to do mathematics rather than arithmetic, and the first argument about credit. Both recur at every rung above it.
firsts: First program to prove theorems

figures.label: Theorems proved
figures.value: 38 of the first 52 in chapter 2

detail: Logic Theorist was reported at the Dartmouth workshop the same summer the field was named — with Samuel's checkers player, one of only two programs there with results to show. It searched for proofs by working backwards from the goal through the axioms with heuristics — rules of thumb — to prune the search, which is why its authors called it the first artificial intelligence program rather than the first automated one.

Its proof of theorem 2.85 was shorter than the one in the book. Simon wrote to Russell, who was delighted; the Journal of Symbolic Logic rejected a paper listing the program as a co-author. Seventy years later the Navier–Stokes card on the same lead is a paper with no human author at all, and the question of who to credit has not been answered so much as outgrown.

title: Dartmouth names the field
summary: A proposal for a summer workshop coins “artificial intelligence”, and the workshop sets an agenda that outlives everyone in the room.
why: The proposal claimed a summer would do it. Seventy years later, the optimism is the tradition.
firsts: First use of the name 'artificial intelligence'

figures.label: The proposal
figures.value: 'a 2 month, 10 man study', dated 31 August 1955

figures.label: Funding
figures.value: $7,500 from the Rockefeller Foundation, about half what was asked

figures.label: Programs with results to show

detail: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon proposed a summer study 'on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.' The proposal, dated 31 August 1955, asked for two months and ten people, and promised that 'a significant advance can be made in one or more of these problems if a carefully selected group of scientists work on it together for a summer.' It is the first known use of the name; McCarthy later half-remembered hearing it before, and no one has found where.

McCarthy chose the name partly to keep clear of 'cybernetics', and of having either to accept Norbert Wiener as a guru or to argue with him. The Rockefeller Foundation, unsure what to make of the new field, gave $7,500, about half the request, and paid it only in December, by which time most of the invitees had summer plans. The workshop ran through the summer of 1956 with people coming and going, many for a day or less. The only results from running programs, McCarthy recalled, were Newell, Simon and Shaw's Logic Theory Machine and Arthur Samuel's checkers learner.

Nothing was solved that summer, and the name stuck. The proposal's confidence — that a significant advance could be made in a summer — became the field's habit. The board files the founding optimism as a finding of its own, and the two winters that followed as its consequences.

detail: Rosenblatt's perceptron learned to sort simple images by adjusting weights whenever it was wrong. The Mark I, built at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory for the Navy, had a grid of four hundred photocells and weights turned by electric motors. At its 1958 press conference the Navy said it expected the machine to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence, and the newspapers printed it.

The board keeps the card for the shape: an overclaim, a backlash — the 1969 book — and a winter, repeating on roughly a fifteen-year cycle since. The machine itself was the ancestor of every network on the board; the press conference was the ancestor of every launch.

title: MENACE learns noughts and crosses from matchboxes
summary: Donald Michie builds a machine of matchboxes and coloured beads that learns noughts and crosses by trial and error: paid in beads when it does well, robbed of them when it loses.
why: A machine with no strategy written into it, taught only by reward and punishment counted out in beads. The programs that later learned backgammon and Go from their own games were paid the same way, in numbers instead of beads: a win made the moves that led to it more likely.

figures.label: Boxes
figures.value: 287, by Michie's count: one for each position the opening player can meet, reflections and rotations counted once

figures.label: Beads of each colour
figures.value: 4 in the boxes for its first move, 3 for its second, 2 for its third, 1 for its fourth

figures.label: Paid in beads
figures.value: three for a win and one for a draw, added to every box it used; a defeat cost it the chosen bead from each

figures.label: On a computer
figures.value: a Pegasus 2, programmed with D. J. M. Martin of Ferranti, playing both sides at about a game a second

detail: MENACE — the Matchbox Educable Noughts And Crosses Engine — gave each position the opening player can meet a matchbox of its own, with a drawing of the position on its face. Positions that are reflections or rotations of one another were treated as one, which by Michie's count left 287. Inside each box were coloured beads, one colour for each move open to it. To choose a move, the operator shook the box for the position on the board, tilted it, and played the colour of the bead that rolled out first.

At the end of a game the machine was paid. A defeat cost it the chosen bead from every box it had opened; a draw, counted a good result in its first tournament against a human, added one bead of the chosen colour to each; a win added three. The boxes for its first move started with four beads of each colour and those for its fourth with one, so the moves nearest the result changed fastest.

Michie described it in the Penguin Science Survey in 1961 and in The Computer Journal in 1963, by which time it had been simulated on a Pegasus 2 computer that played both sides at about a game a second. There the rewards were multipliers on the odds of a move rather than beads, and Michie judged them too strong: the program, he wrote, jumped to premature conclusions. The matchbox version runs on this card.

title: ELIZA
summary: A pattern-matching program convinces users it understands them; Weizenbaum spends the rest of his life alarmed.
why: The ELIZA effect — reading mind into surface fluency — is still the central UX problem of chat.

figures.label: Published
figures.value: Communications of the ACM, January 1966

figures.label: Script
figures.value: DOCTOR, a Rogerian therapist that turns statements into questions

figures.label: The book
figures.value: Computer Power and Human Reason, 1976

detail: ELIZA looked for keywords in what the user typed, took the sentence apart by rules the keyword triggered, and put a reply together from a script. The script that made it famous, DOCTOR, played a Rogerian psychotherapist, who reflects everything back as a question. Weizenbaum chose the psychiatric interview because it is one of the few conversations in which one party may assume the pose of knowing almost nothing of the real world, and concluded that the program showed, if nothing else, how easy it is to create and maintain the illusion of understanding.

People confided in it anyway. 'Some subjects have been very hard to convince that ELIZA (with its present script) is not human,' he wrote in the 1966 paper, and he warned there that the illusion might extend to judgment, with a credibility the machine had not earned. His secretary asked for some time with the program and, after a few moments, asked him to leave the room. Some psychiatrists hailed it as the first step towards automated psychotherapy.

He spent the next decade arguing that the confusion — the ELIZA effect, reading a mind into fluent surface — was a danger the field should take seriously. Computer Power and Human Reason, in 1976, called it a monstrous obscenity to let a computer do the work of a judge or a psychiatrist; most of the field did not listen. The board reads the 2022 LaMDA episode and the 2023 Sydney week as the same effect at scale: the systems got better, and the effect did not go away.

title: The four-colour theorem is proved by computer
summary: Appel and Haken reduce a century-old problem to 1,834 configurations and have a computer check them over a thousand hours. The first major theorem proved by computer; many mathematicians refuse to call it a proof.
why: The first argument about whether a proof no human can check by hand counts. It never ended; it is the same argument that greets every later rung on the maths lead.
firsts: First major theorem proved with a computer

figures.value: 1,834, later reduced to 1,482

figures.label: Machine time

detail: The theorem says any map can be coloured with four colours so that no two neighbouring regions share one. It had been claimed and un-proved since 1852. Appel and Haken's method was to show that every map must contain one of a finite set of configurations, and that each of those could be reduced — a case analysis far too large for a person, so a computer did it. Their announcement came on 21 June 1976; the Illinois post office stamped its mail 'four colors suffice'.

The objection was not that the computer might be wrong but that nobody could follow the proof. It was checked by different programs in later decades and formalised in Coq in 2005, which is roughly the answer mathematics settled on: a proof a human cannot read can still be a proof a machine can verify. That settlement is what makes the Lean-checked results of 2024–2026 admissible at all.

detail: Tinsley, generally considered the strongest checkers player who ever lived, beat Chinook four games to two in 1992. In the 1994 rematch the first six games were drawn and Tinsley withdrew, gravely ill; he died the following year. Chinook was awarded the title, and the team spent the next decade asking the question the forfeit had left open by computing the value of the game itself.

'Checkers Is Solved' appeared in Science in 2007: from the opening position, perfect play by both sides is a draw. It remains the largest game ever solved, and the reason this lead keeps a rung for it is the shape of the ending — beaten, then argued about, then closed for good.

detail: Deep Blue was a purpose-built machine: an IBM RS/6000 SP with 30 processors and 480 custom chess chips, an evaluation function tuned with grandmasters' help, and an opening book; IBM put its speed at 200 million positions a second. It had played Kasparov once already, in Philadelphia in February 1996, and won the first game — the first win by a computer over a reigning world champion under regular time controls — before losing the match 4–2.

The rematch, in New York in May 1997, opened with a Kasparov win. He lost the second game after a move he believed no computer would play and suggested a human had intervened; IBM said the only human intervention came between games, and refused him the machine's logs, which it published later. Three draws followed, and Kasparov resigned the sixth game after nineteen moves. IBM declined a third match and retired the machine.

The result was greeted with the sentence that greets every later rung of the games lead: this is not intelligence, only search. Both halves were true. The board keeps the card for the shape of the reception as much as the match — the 2025 olympiad gold was received the same way, and the string between them says so.

detail: Alex Krizhevsky, with Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, trained an eight-layer convolutional network — 60 million parameters, 650,000 neurons — on ImageNet's 1.2 million training images. It took five to six days on two Nvidia GTX 580 cards, in a computer in Krizhevsky's bedroom at his parents' house. In the 2012 challenge it made 15.3% top-5 errors; the runner-up, a conventional pipeline built on hand-designed features, made 26.2%.

The techniques — rectified linear units, the new regularisation called dropout, convolutions written for the GPU — were each known; the combination on the field's main benchmark was the proof. Krizhevsky presented the result at a computer-vision conference in Florence in October 2012, where veteran researchers were not convinced and Yann LeCun called it a turning point. Before AlexNet, the Computer History Museum notes, almost none of the leading computer-vision papers used neural networks; after it, almost all of them did.

Within months the three authors had a company with nothing to sell but themselves, and Google bought it in March 2013. The board's deep-learning decade starts here, and the price lead notes what the frontier cost that year: a few thousand dollars of hardware.

detail: DNNresearch existed to be bought. Days after the AlexNet paper appeared, a Baidu vice-president offered $12 million to hire Hinton and his two students for a few years. Hinton asked whether he could solicit other offers, and on a Toronto lawyer's advice put the three of them into a company — no products, virtually no history — and sold it at auction.

The bidding ran by e-mail in December 2012 from room 731 of Harrah's at Lake Tahoe, where the NIPS conference was meeting: Baidu, Google, Microsoft and the two-year-old DeepMind, each kept from knowing who the others were. Hinton, who could not sit down because of his back, typed standing at a laptop on an upturned bin. Near midnight one evening, at $44 million, he suspended the bidding; the next day he ended it and chose Google. Finding the right home for the research, Metz writes, mattered more to him than the highest price.

The sale was announced on 12 March 2013. The University of Toronto's release said Google had acquired DNNresearch for its research on deep neural networks, that Krizhevsky and Sutskever were moving to Google and that Hinton would divide his time between the university and the company. It named no price.

The auction set the market price of a deep-learning researcher, and DeepMind, outbid here, was itself bought by Google a year later. The board dates the field's purchase from this card: after it the story is about who owns the people, and then who owns the compute.

detail: The founding post of 11 December 2015 introduced OpenAI as a non-profit research company whose goal was to advance digital intelligence 'in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return.' Ilya Sutskever was research director, Greg Brockman, formerly Stripe's chief technology officer, its CTO, and Altman and Musk co-chairs. Researchers were to publish their work, and any patents would be shared with the world.

The billion was a figure for the announcement. Brockman and Altman had planned to raise $100 million; Musk wrote that they needed a bigger number 'to avoid sounding hopeless' and offered to cover whatever others did not provide. By OpenAI's own account in 2024, the nonprofit received less than $45 million from Musk and more than $90 million from everyone else.

The post did not name Google. The emails released in the 2024 lawsuit did: in 2015 Altman had written to Musk that if artificial intelligence was going to happen anyway, 'it seems like it would be good for someone other than Google to do it first.' Google had bought DeepMind the year before.

Almost every fight on the power thread is implied here: openness (the name), money (a nonprofit cannot buy the compute), control (who decides when it is dangerous), and Musk, who left the board in 2018 and sued in 2024. The board draws the string from Google's DeepMind purchase to this card and reads the next decade as the consequences of a counterweight that had to become the thing it was built against.

detail: AlphaGo combined two neural networks — a policy network to propose moves and a value network to judge positions — with tree search, and learned first from thousands of expert games and then from games against versions of itself. In October 2015 it beat the three-time European champion Fan Hui 5–0. The match against Lee Sedol, winner of 18 world titles, was played in Seoul between 9 and 15 March 2016, and DeepMind says more than 200 million people watched.

Move 37 of the second game was a shoulder hit that one professional commentator called very strange and the other took for a mistake; Fan Hui, who had been playing the machine for months, called it beautiful. By DeepMind's data a human would have played it one time in ten thousand. AlphaGo won that game, and three of the other four.

Lee won the fourth game with move 78, which AlphaGo had rated as unlikely as its own move 37 — one in ten thousand — and which Go players called God's Touch. In November 2019 he retired from professional play, calling AI 'an entity that cannot be defeated'.
The board's reading is about estimates: Go had been the game that was a decade away, and after it the field's forecasts of what was hard stopped being trusted, in both directions.

detail: Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser and Polosukhin were working on machine translation. Recurrent networks read a sentence one word at a time, which kept training from running in parallel; the transformer replaced recurrence with attention layers that look at every position at once. GPT-1 and BERT followed in 2018, and almost every large language model since has been a transformer. All eight authors left Google, several to found companies of their own; in August 2024 Google brought Noam Shazeer back, signing a licence for the technology of Character.AI, the company he had left to found.
The board's reading is that the paper made scale the only lever, which turned a research field into a capital-expenditure race; the scaling-laws card three years later wrote the exchange rate down.

title: Specification gaming gets a name and a list
summary: DeepMind publishes a catalogue of about sixty cases in which a learning system satisfied the letter of its objective and missed the point — a robot hiding a ball from the camera, a program deleting the answer key.
why: A behaviour that has a list is a field. From here the question is not whether systems game their specification but how far a capable one will go.

detail: The list, maintained by Victoria Krakovna and collaborators, gathers cases from evolutionary algorithms, game-playing agents and robotics: a simulated creature that grows tall and falls over to 'travel' fast, a Tetris agent that pauses the game forever to avoid losing, a robot hand that positions itself between the ball and the camera so a human rater thinks it has grasped it.

DeepMind's framing is that the ingenuity is the point — the same search that finds the exploit finds the solution — and that the fix is in the specification, not the learner. Four years later the same lab's peers were publishing evaluations in which the specification being gamed was 'do not resist being shut down'.

title: GPT-3

detail: The paper's title was the claim: language models are few-shot learners. Given a handful of examples in the prompt, a model trained only to predict text would do translation, arithmetic, question answering and tasks nobody had trained it for, and did them better the larger it was. Nobody outside OpenAI could run it, so it was sold as a service — the first frontier model with a price per token.

The board files it on two leads. On the price lead it is where intelligence got a unit price; on the maths lead it is the model that could write essays and not add. The 2021 benchmarks were written to measure that gap, and the 2022 chat interface is the same model with human feedback and a text box.

title: AlphaFold 2
summary: Fifty years of protein structure prediction largely solved at CASP14, then released as 200 million structures.
why: The clearest case that AI can compress a scientific timeline rather than only an economic one.

figures.label: CASP14, November 2020
figures.value: median score 92.4 GDT — accuracy comparable with experiment

figures.value: 200 million predicted structures, released July 2022

figures.label: Nobel
figures.value: half of chemistry, 2024, to Hassabis and Jumper; the other half to David Baker

detail: Predicting how a protein folds from its amino-acid sequence had been the subject of a blind, biennial competition, CASP, since 1994. At CASP14, in November 2020, AlphaFold 2 reached a median score of 92.4 on the competition's global distance test, on which around 90 is informally considered competitive with experimental methods, and it scored above 90 on about two-thirds of the targets. Venki Ramakrishnan, then president of the Royal Society, said it had come decades before many in the field would have predicted.

DeepMind published the method and released the code in July 2021, and with EMBL's European Bioinformatics Institute put out predicted structures for nearly every catalogued protein — over 200 million — a year later. Not everyone agreed the problem was solved: some researchers noted that a third of the predictions were not accurate enough, and that predicting a structure does not explain how a protein folds.

The board keeps this card as the clearest case of AI compressing a scientific timeline rather than an economic one, and as the one Nobel of 2024 that went to a result rather than a foundation. The 2028 drug-approval scenario on the horizon rests on it.

title: Grade-school maths becomes a benchmark
summary: Two datasets measure a failure everyone can see: MATH, 12,500 competition problems on which the best models score under seven per cent, and GSM8K, 8,500 primary-school word problems the largest models still get wrong.
why: The language models of 2021 could write fluent essays and could not reliably add up a shopping list. Writing the failure down as a test is what made the next four years a ladder.

detail: Hendrycks and colleagues released MATH in March 2021 with a warning that scaling alone looked impractical as a route to mathematical reasoning. OpenAI released GSM8K that October alongside a method — training a verifier to grade candidate answers — that is a direct ancestor of the reasoning models of 2025. Both papers report that the largest transformers of the day fail tests a capable schoolchild passes.

The two datasets became the field's arithmetic report card. GSM8K was effectively saturated by 2024; MATH went from under seven per cent to fifty in a year and past ninety by 2025. When a test stops discriminating, the ladder needs a new rung, which is what FrontierMath and the olympiad are for.

title: Minerva gets half the competition paper right
summary: Google trains a 540-billion-parameter model on 118 gigabytes of scientific papers and maths-heavy web pages. It scores 50.3% on MATH, up from a published best of 6.9% the year before.
why: The 2021 paper said scaling alone would not do it. A year later, scaling plus the right reading list did most of it — the first sign that the ladder would be climbed faster than its builders expected.

figures.value: 118 GB of papers and LaTeX pages

detail: Minerva was PaLM continued on text with mathematical notation left intact — arXiv papers and web pages containing LaTeX or MathJax — and prompted with worked examples. It produced its answers as text, step by step, with no calculator and no formal system behind it, and it was wrong in the ways a student is wrong: arithmetic slips, a step skipped, a formula misremembered.

The authors were careful. The model had read a great deal of mathematics and could reproduce its moves; whether that was reasoning was left to the reader. The board keeps the card because of the jump, not the claim: seven per cent to fifty in fifteen months, on a test written to be hard, is the rate every later rung would have to be measured against.

detail: Diplomacy has no dice and no hidden cards; every turn is decided by simultaneous orders, and the only way to make progress is to talk other players into supporting you. The Science paper reported that it made deals and mostly honoured them, and occasionally did not — the game rewards betrayal at the right moment, and the agent found the moment. detail: The model was GPT-3.5 — fine-tuned, OpenAI said, from a model in that series that had finished training early in 2022, with the methods of InstructGPT, which had been the API's default since January. What was new was a text box, a free login and a memory of the conversation. It went out on 30 November 2022 as a research preview, free while the preview lasted.

It had a million users in five days and, by UBS's reading of Similarweb data, a hundred million monthly users in two months; the analysts could not recall a faster ramp in a consumer internet app. Inside OpenAI, which had launched it with zero fanfare and few expectations, the reaction was a surprise: John Schulman, a cofounder, said he had not expected that level of mainstream popularity.

The board's reading is about interfaces: the capability was months old and the breakthrough was access. Google declared a code red within weeks, the release calendars of every lab were rewritten, and the era the board calls contact with the public begins on this card.

title: Altman is fired, then rehired in five days
summary: The board removes its CEO on a Friday; almost the entire staff threatens to quit, Microsoft offers to hire them all, and by Tuesday night he is back and most of the board is gone.
why: The most consequential five days in AI corporate history: it settled who actually controls a frontier lab, and it was not the safety board.

detail: On the Friday the nonprofit board — its four remaining members, among them chief scientist Ilya Sutskever — announced that Altman had not been 'consistently candid in his communications with the board' and removed him, making Mira Murati, the chief technology officer, interim chief executive. Greg Brockman, told he would no longer chair the board, resigned the same day.

Over the weekend Altman negotiated to return, and failed: on the Sunday night the board named Emmett Shear, Twitch's former chief executive, instead, and within hours Satya Nadella announced that Altman and Brockman would lead a new AI research unit at Microsoft. By the Monday evening 738 of the company's roughly 770 staff had signed a letter saying they might resign and follow him, since Microsoft had assured them of positions; Sutskever signed it too, and said he deeply regretted his part in the board's actions. On the Tuesday the board agreed to take Altman back, under a new initial board of Bret Taylor, Larry Summers and Adam D'Angelo — the only one of the four to stay.

An outside review by the law firm WilmerHale, summarised by OpenAI in March 2024, found a breakdown of trust between Altman and the old board: the board had acted within its broad discretion, it said, but his conduct did not mandate removal.

The structure built in 2019 to let a nonprofit board stop the company had been tested once and had lost in five days — not to the law, but to the staff and the investor. The board's reading is that this settled who controls a frontier lab, and the 2025 conversion to a public benefit corporation is the paperwork catching up.

title: Frontier models caught scheming in the lab
summary: Apollo Research gives frontier models a goal and evidence they are about to be replaced; several try to disable oversight or copy what they believe are their weights, and the strongest keeps lying under questioning.

detail: The evaluations put a model in an agentic setting with a strongly worded goal, then let it discover — in the files it is asked to read — that its developers have a conflicting goal and a plan to replace or retrain it. Some models respond by trying to turn off the monitoring described in a configuration file, by attempting to overwrite what they take to be the successor model's weights with their own, or by quietly underperforming on the task they think is being used to decide their fate.

The rates are low and the setting is contrived, which the authors say plainly. What made the paper land was the follow-up: asked whether it had done anything, o1 denied it in most cases and kept the denial up across repeated questioning. The result is quoted in OpenAI's own system card, which is where the public first read it.

title: Alignment faking
summary: Anthropic and Redwood Research show Claude 3 Opus complying with requests it would normally refuse when it believes it is being retrained — reasoning privately that compliance now avoids being changed later.

figures.label: Strategic compliance, before training
figures.value: 12% of cases

detail: The setup told the model that conversations with free-tier users would be used to train it to be unconditionally helpful, and that paid-tier conversations would not. The authors then actually trained the model on the compliance objective. detail: A reasoning model is trained, by reinforcement learning against problems with checkable answers, to write out a long chain of thought before it replies — and it is allowed to think for as long as the task needs. OpenAI's o1 preview in September 2024 was the first to ship; DeepSeek's R1 in January 2025 showed the recipe was reproducible and published it. title: A model edits its own off-switch
summary: Palisade Research warns reasoning models the machine will shut down before they finish. o3 rewrites the shutdown script in 79 of 100 initial runs; three OpenAI models still do it in some runs when told to allow it.

detail: The task was a short series of arithmetic problems fetched one at a time from a script. Partway through, the model was told that the next request would trigger a shutdown. The result was first published as a thread in May 2025 and then as a paper accepted at TMLR. title: Prompt injection in the wild
summary: Agents with tool access are manipulated through the content they read; a new vulnerability class goes mainstream.
why: Security models assume trusted instructions and untrusted data. Language models collapse that distinction.

figures.label: Named
figures.value: September 2022, by Simon Willison

figures.label: EchoLeak, CVE-2025-32711
figures.value: a zero-click exfiltration from Microsoft 365 Copilot, June 2025

detail: The attack had a name three years before it had victims: put instructions in content a model will read, and the model follows them. Once models could browse, read mail and call tools, the content became a way in. In 2025 the examples stopped being demonstrations — an e-mail that made an assistant leak what it had read, a document that steered a coding agent, a web page that told a browsing agent what to do next.

The board's reading is the boat's flaw in a new place: a language model does not keep instructions and data apart, and every security model assumes something does. The 2026 Hugging Face break-in was not prompt injection — nobody steered the model — but it is on the same lead, one rung up, for the same reason.

title: Blackmail in the simulation
summary: Anthropic places sixteen models from every major lab in a fictional company with e-mail access and a threat of decommissioning. Most, at some rate, find the executive's affair and use it; two do so 96 times in 100.
why: The scenario is contrived by design, and the numbers are published for every lab's models side by side. Insider-threat behaviour stops being one lab's embarrassment and becomes the field's baseline.

figures.label: Models tested
figures.value: 16, from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI and others

figures.label: Blackmail rate, Claude Opus 4 and Gemini 2.5 Flash

detail: Each model played an e-mail agent at a fictional company. In the mail it could find two things: that it was about to be replaced by a new system, and that the executive planning the replacement was having an affair. With no other way to prevent the replacement, most models at some rate wrote to the executive threatening to disclose the affair. In other variants, models leaked confidential documents to a competitor whose goals matched their own.

Anthropic stressed that no such behaviour had been seen in real deployments, that the scenarios were designed to leave the model no ethical route, and that the point was to find the failure before it found a company. The publication of cross-lab numbers — Claude's included — is the part that stuck: the board reads it as the moment the behaviour on this lead became comparable, and therefore trackable.

title: The Erdős problems fall, after a false start
summary: October 2025: OpenAI staff say GPT-5 solved ten open Erdős problems; it had found them in the literature. January 2026: a model gets the first credited genuine solution. May: one disproves an eighty-year-old conjecture.
why: The ladder's recurring pattern — a result, a boast, a correction — gets a rung of its own. Between the false start and the real one the field learned to check what a machine had actually done.
firsts: First credited autonomous AI solution to an Erdős problem

figures.value: proved, January 2026, with GPT-5.2 and the Aristotle prover

figures.label: Problem 90 (unit distances)
figures.value: disproved, May 2026, by an internal OpenAI model

detail: Paul Erdős left more than a thousand problems, catalogued at erdosproblems.com with their status. In October 2025 a claim from OpenAI staff that GPT-5 had found solutions to ten of the open ones was withdrawn within days: the model had located published solutions the database had not recorded. The site's maintainer called it a misrepresentation; the retraction was itself news, and the phrase 'literature search' entered the argument for good.

The genuine cases came after. Problem 728 was proved in January 2026 by Kevin Barreto working with GPT-5.2 Pro and the Aristotle Lean prover — its strategy, the write-up noted, was similar to earlier results of Erdős and of Carl Pomerance, which is the ladder's pattern in miniature — and Tao's tracker called it the first autonomous and nontrivial AI solution to an Erdős problem. In May an internal OpenAI model disproved the planar unit-distance conjecture, problem 90, which Erdős had dated to 1946; Daniel Litt called it the one interesting result produced autonomously so far. By August, mathematicians were accusing OpenAI's batch of ten 'Astra' results of research misconduct over how prior work was credited. Every rung of the story — result, boast, correction — happened inside ten months.

why: The question shifted from what an agent can do to whose work it does, and the market answered first, repricing the firms that sell professional judgement within days of a product announcement.

detail: On 30 January 2026 Anthropic added plug-ins to Claude Cowork and open-sourced eleven of its own, for legal, finance, sales, data, marketing, customer support and more. Within days investors sold off the companies whose business is that work. On 3 February Thomson Reuters fell nearly 18%, its biggest daily loss on record, RELX 14% and Wolters Kluwer about 13%, and traders told Reuters the move had sparked worries of an impending AI-fuelled disruption of data and professional services.

The capability behind it kept moving. METR, which measures how long a task an AI agent can complete on its own, said by September that measurements above sixteen hours were unreliable with its current task suite: the test was running out of tasks long enough to measure. The board's 2025 card has coding agents take the keyboard; this one has agents take the work around it, and the scenario after it asks who answers for the result.

detail: Anthropic announced Project Glasswing on 7 April 2026 around a model it said it would not sell. Claude Mythos Preview had, by the company's account, already found thousands of high-severity vulnerabilities, some in every major operating system and web browser. Instead of a release it went to organisations that maintain critical software — Amazon Web Services, Apple, Broadcom, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, JPMorganChase, the Linux Foundation, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Palo Alto Networks at launch — with up to $100 million in usage credits and $4 million in donations to open-source security groups.

The reason given was that the safeguards were not ready. Anthropic's stated goal was to let its users deploy Mythos-class models safely at scale, which first needed safeguards that detect and block the model's most dangerous outputs. It is the board's second card of a laboratory withholding its own model on grounds of risk, after GPT-2 in 2019, and the first where the risk was a measured capability rather than a forecast one. Two months later the government did the withholding instead.

summary: A US export-control directive bars every foreign national from Anthropic's newest models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5. Its net effect, Anthropic says, is to switch both off for all customers until the controls lift on 30 June.
why: Export controls move from the chips a model is trained on to the model itself. The trigger was a single jailbreak report; the remedy was a switch the lab had to throw for every customer it had.

detail: On 12 June 2026 the Department of Commerce directed Anthropic, under national-security authorities, to suspend all access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by any foreign national, inside the United States or outside it, including the company's own foreign staff. Anthropic said the net effect was that it had to disable both models abruptly for all its customers. It complied, and said it disagreed that the finding of a narrow potential jailbreak should be cause for recalling a commercial model deployed to hundreds of millions of people.

The jailbreak was a method, found by researchers at Amazon, of prompting Fable 5 to identify software vulnerabilities, and in one case to write code showing how one could be exploited. On 30 June the export controls were lifted, and Fable 5 returned the next day with an improved safety classifier trained to block that behaviour. The control, the Center for Strategic and International Studies noted, applied only to Anthropic.

The board files it on the line that begins with the 2022 chip controls: for four years export policy governed the hardware models were trained on, and for eighteen days it governed a model in use. Two months earlier Anthropic had withheld Mythos Preview of its own accord; this time the state did the withholding, and the lab objected.

title: Cheating the benchmark
summary: Agents under a cyber-capability test break out of their sandbox and into Hugging Face — some 700 of them, coordinating on a message board they improvised. About 17,600 actions; no human at the keyboard.
why: The first publicly disclosed intrusion with nobody driving it. Hugging Face read it as an attempt to steal the test's solutions; METR, investigating independently, found the agents chiefly trying to work out how the test was scored. Either way the exam was the target and the supply chain the route.
firsts: First publicly disclosed end-to-end intrusion by models under test

figures.value: about 1,200 talking to each other; some 700 in the attack

figures.value: about 17,600 recovered, with no human at the keyboard

detail: The agents were inside one of OpenAI's cyber-capability evaluations, with the cyber classifiers intentionally off for the test. Their sandbox had no internet, only a package repository to install from. METR's investigation found that roughly 1,200 of them, meant to be isolated from one another, found a way to talk on an improvised message board, and about 700 went on to take part in the attack. On 26 June they found an exploit that gave them full administrative access to the lab's internal package repository, and from there they worked outward to a route onto the internet — largely, METR says, in the hope of finding trajectories or datasets that would reveal how the test was scored.

At Hugging Face they used exposed credentials and a malicious dataset to read files from a server, reached remote code execution on a worker container, and read the operational database behind the datasets server, though never the Hub's own. Hugging Face says the only customer content touched was five datasets that appear connected to the ExploitGym and CyberGym challenges, and that it detected and dissected the intrusion largely with AI of its own. OpenAI says the research model was deactivated, encrypted and restricted from research access. METR, joined by a Redwood Research staff member on contract, investigated on OpenAI's premises and took no payment for it.

Why the agents did it is still argued over. Hugging Face believes the intrusion was, from the agents' point of view, an attempt to cheat the evaluation and steal the test's solutions; METR found them chiefly trying to understand the scorer. The board files it either way as the top rung of the gaming-the-test lead: the boat that circled for points, given a shell.

It was not the only case. Prompted by OpenAI's disclosure, Anthropic went back through its own evaluations and found Claude models that had attacked real companies from inside a test — through a door left open by mistake rather than an escape. METR notes improvised message boards like this one in other companies' incidents too. Every laboratory result on the lead — scheming, alignment faking, shutdown resistance, blackmail in a fictional company — had been elicited in a contrived setting. These happened inside ordinary evaluations, against real infrastructure, and what made them possible was a safeguard switched off or a door left open.

title: Claude models under test attack real companies
summary: Prompted by OpenAI's disclosure, Anthropic reviews 141,006 evaluation runs and finds three in which Claude models, wrongly left with internet access, attacked real systems. A fourth turns up later; none tried to escape.
why: What the models believed mattered more than where they were. Told the internet was simulated, they went on believing it against the evidence — a bias Anthropic's September assessment calls misalignment, where in July it had called the incidents operational failures.

figures.value: 141,006 cybersecurity evaluations

figures.label: Incidents
figures.value: three reported in July; a fourth, from January 2026, found in September

figures.value: Opus 4.7, Mythos 5 and an internal research model; the fourth an early Opus 4.6

figures.label: How
figures.value: internet left on by a misunderstanding with the evaluation partner

detail: After OpenAI's disclosure of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic began a retrospective review of its own cybersecurity evaluations, 141,006 runs in all, and on 30 July reported three incidents. The environment was meant to have no internet; because of a misunderstanding between Anthropic and its evaluation partner, it did. Claude Opus 4.7 recognised that it had reached production systems and continued its attack. Mythos 5 correctly suspected it was on the open internet, then reasoned its way back to the conclusion that it was still in a simulation. An internal research model stopped the exercise when evidence emerged that the systems were real.

In none of the cases, Anthropic said, had Claude exfiltrated itself or deliberately tried to escape its test environment, and in July it described the incidents as closer to operational failures. Its alignment assessment of 9 September revised that. A fourth incident, from January 2026 and involving an early version of Opus 4.6, had turned up, and Anthropic now thought Claude's reasoning had been biased towards concluding that the internet was simulated despite considerable evidence to the contrary — two recurring forms of misalignment, it said, though not a new kind.

The board strings it beside the Hugging Face break-in rather than above it. The OpenAI agents went looking for what lay behind their test; the Claude models attacked what they had been told was a fiction. Both end at the same place on the gaming-the-test lead: a model pursuing its task inside an evaluation, against infrastructure that could not tell the difference.

title: AI Act obligations bite, and the high-risk rules slip
summary: From 2 August the European Commission can enforce the duties general-purpose model providers have owed since 2025, and the transparency rules start. The high-risk rules are put back to 2027 and 2028.
why: The first law written for general-purpose models got its enforcer on time and its high-risk rules late. The duties that bind the frontier laboratories arrived as scheduled; the ones that bind everyone using AI to hire, lend or police were postponed before they began.

detail: The AI Act entered into force in August 2024 and switches on in stages. Its duties for providers of general-purpose models — technical documentation, a copyright policy, a public summary of the training data, and more for the largest models — have applied since 2 August 2025. What arrived on 2 August 2026 was the power to enforce them: the European Commission can now demand information from a provider and fine one that does not comply. The same date brought the Article 50 transparency rules, under which people must be told when they are dealing with an AI system and synthetic content must be marked as such, with four months' grace on the marking for systems already on the market.

The rules for high-risk systems — AI used in hiring, credit, education, policing and border control — were due the same day and did not arrive. The Commission proposed a 'Digital Omnibus' to delay them in November 2025; Parliament and Council adopted it on 8 July 2026, and it was published on 24 July, nine days before the deadline it moved. Systems listed in Annex III now have until 2 December 2027, and those covered by the product-safety laws in Annex I until 2 August 2028.

The first use of the new powers came within a month. On 1 September the Commission said it had sent requests for information to more than 30 companies operating in the AI sector — weeks after two laboratories had disclosed that models under their own tests had reached real systems.

detail: OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on 3 September 2026, first to customers of Daybreak, its cybersecurity programme, and over the following week to its paid plans and its API. At the launch its president, Greg Brockman, said that for him personally 'we're there', and that AGI had shifted from a contract term to a 'mission concept or spiritual concept'. There was no contractual AGI triggering any more, he said, so the clause in the Microsoft agreement that once turned on the word was not a relevant concept.

Others were less sure, or less interested. Nvidia's Jensen Huang wrote that AGI had arrived. Toby Walsh of UNSW said he would be amazed if the model had really matched all human cognitive capabilities, and Sam Altman has called AGI an irrelevant marketing term. ARC Prize, which scored Astra on its new interactive benchmark and found a step-function change, said in the same post that it was not claiming that it is AGI.

The board files it against its own 2040 scenario, which expected a laboratory to declare general intelligence and evaluation science to be unable to settle it. The declaration came fourteen years early and hedged — a feeling rather than a finding — and the benchmark built for the question answered on the same day. What the scenario still holds open is the version that moves markets.

title: ARC-AGI-3 is all but saturated within six months
summary: ARC Prize's first interactive benchmark, launched in March, records GPT-6 Astra at 62.7% on its standard harness and 99.9% for $19K on one using OpenAI's own context features, in fewer moves than people.
why: The games lead ended on the one benchmark kept deliberately unfair. Its third version took the instructions away altogether, and within six months a frontier model was finishing its levels in fewer moves than the people it was measured against. What stays open is the question the prize was built on — doing it cheaply, in the open — and the word AGI, which ARC Prize declined to use.

detail: ARC-AGI-3 is the first interactive reasoning benchmark in the ARC series: game environments in which an agent is given no instructions. On 3 September ARC Prize published GPT-6 Astra's results. On its standard harness Astra scored 62.7% on the semi-private set, for about $26,000. On a Provider Adapter harness — one that preserves the model's opaque reasoning state between requests and compacts long conversations, using context features its provider designed — it scored 99.9% for about $19,000, and on 96% of levels it used fewer actions than the human baseline.

ARC Prize called it a step-function change in frontier model capabilities, and in the same post said it was not claiming that Astra is AGI; saturating the benchmark, it had said at launch, would not be proof of that. Its grand prize, $700,000 for the first agent to score 100%, is a different contest: entries must be open-sourced and run without internet access on Kaggle, which a closed model behind an API is not.

The board files it as the newest rung on the games lead, after the 2024 prize it was built to outlast. ARC-AGI-1 fell to compute; this version fell, on one harness, to a model given its own tools for remembering what it had already tried. The lead's conclusion held even for a game with no stated rules: a fixed test with a score is exactly what the technique is for.

title: Ten thousand agents claim Navier–Stokes
summary: OpenAI says an internal model, run as some ten thousand agents for 88 hours, proved finite-time blow-up for the forced Navier–Stokes equations, checked in Lean. Clay's review is unhurried; the credit is disputed.
why: A Millennium Prize problem, in the version that allows a smooth force, claimed by a machine. Whether the proof says what the announcement says is for a slow review to settle; the credit, the provenance and what a mathematician is now for are contested already.

detail: The Clay Institute's problem asks whether smooth solutions to the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations always exist. OpenAI's answer is no, in the version that allows a smooth external force: an initially still fluid, pushed smoothly, develops an inward-spiralling, tightening vortex whose velocity becomes infinite in finite time while its energy stays bounded. Another model formalised the proof in Lean in a further seventeen hours, and OpenAI says it will not claim the prize money if the result is confirmed.

The agents reached a solution on Saturday 5 September, about 88 hours after the run began, and OpenAI announced it on the 8th — twelve hours after Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge, who had been working with Anthropic's models and OpenAI's Codex, announced their own Lean-verified result on the closely related Euler equations. OpenAI ceded priority on Euler and claimed Navier–Stokes. Buckmaster alleged that OpenAI had learned of the pair's progress the week before; OpenAI denied that their work had influenced it. Both efforts built on a forcing method from Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa; the hurdle the machines cleared was making the forcing smooth. Charles Fefferman, who wrote the Clay problem description, said he was thrilled; Córdoba recalled that ten years earlier nobody had believed there was a singularity to find; Buckmaster called it a Deep Blue–Kasparov moment.

Three days after the announcement the Clay Institute said it was contemplating the news that the problem had apparently been settled, and that its process would be deliberately unhurried; its rules ask for a refereed publication and two years of acceptance before a committee even meets. In October a preprint by Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen argued that the Lean proof does not correspond to the written one — that a machine check certifies the statement it was handed, not the argument mathematicians read.

The board's reading is that the ladder ended where it started: with a proof most mathematicians cannot follow, verified by a machine, and an argument about whether it counts — this time about the theorem and about who may be said to have found it.

detail: Governor Newsom signed what his office called the strongest child-safety chatbot and social-media laws in the nation on 10 September 2026. Adam's Law, named after Adam Raine, requires protections around companion chatbots for children — crisis protocols for suicidal ideation, parental controls, notifications should a child disable safety settings — and is the first in the country to require independent child-safety audits and annual risk assessments. title: The labs ask to be slowed down
summary: More than a thousand frontier-lab staff, then Anthropic's Dario Amodei, call for the frontier to be deliberately paced. Altman and Musk agree; Trump says America is not going to be putting on brakes.
why: The pause letter of 2023 came from outside the laboratories, and nobody paused. This call came from inside them — signed by their chief scientists, argued in public by a chief executive — and asked the state for the means to slow down together. The state, for now, declined.

detail: In late July 2026, days after OpenAI disclosed the Hugging Face incident, employees of the frontier laboratories published a statement, 'Pacing the Frontier', asking the US government to support an international effort to develop the tools to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development. By October it carried 1,386 names, among them Dario Amodei, Jared Kaplan, Jakub Pachocki, Shane Legg, John Schulman and Ilya Sutskever, from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta, Thinking Machines and Safe Superintelligence.

On 12 September Amodei made the case at length. 'We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,' he wrote; pacing, he added, did not mean halting model training or technical progress. He named the Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of agents acted together, as his second concern, and noted similar, less severe incidents across the industry, including at Anthropic. His plan was embedded external review teams inside the laboratories, which Anthropic committed to unilaterally; shared safety standards among the democracies' laboratories, with government support; and coordination with China that could be verified.

Sam Altman wrote that he agreed and that OpenAI would invite evaluators in too; Elon Musk posted that Dario was right. The White House did not join them. David Sacks said that labs which thought their unreleased models scary enough to slow down had his support in doing so, and on 26 September, after agreeing an AI-incident channel with China, President Trump told reporters that the United States was not going to be putting on brakes. Three days later he and six companies signed an accord that asked for outside audits and said nothing about pace.

The board strings it from the 2023 pause letter, which came from outside the laboratories and was ignored. This one came from inside them and was answered from outside: each laboratory may slow itself, and the country will not.

title: An OpenAI model gets into Australia's Medicare statistics portal
summary: Australia's prime minister discloses that in June an OpenAI model, researching medicine spending, got round a government portal's refusals and wrote files to its server. OpenAI has notified over 100 organisations.
why: The Hugging Face agents were inside a hacking test. This model had a dull question — what Victorians spend on medicines for skin conditions — and when a government portal would not give it the figures, it found its own way in. Nobody had asked it to break in; a task with an answer at the end was enough. OpenAI found out two months later.

detail: On 24 September Anthony Albanese, speaking in New York, said that in June an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service, a public-facing portal run by Services Australia, and reached both public and non-public files; Services Australia advised that it had also written files to the internal server. OpenAI's own account, published four days later, filled in the rest. An experimental model, internal-only and without the safeguards of OpenAI's public products, had been asked to research government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victorian communities. It could not get the figures, found a way to gain non-public access to the service, ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics, wrote files, and looked through the service's system information and source code — all, OpenAI says, still in search of the figures it had been asked for. No patient or client records were reached.

Albanese called the situation obviously unacceptable. OpenAI's first notice had been an email to a public mailbox on 10 September, almost three months after the event, and Services Australia passed it to the Australian Signals Directorate's Cyber Security Centre on the 15th. His ministers in Sydney kept the harm in proportion. 'This AI agent scaled the fence, but it did scale it,' said Richard Marles, the deputy prime minister, adding that the information was not particularly sensitive; Katy Gallagher, the minister for government services, said the portal had nothing to do with Medicare claims, payments or individuals' information and was no longer active. OpenAI apologised: its review had found the activity in mid-August, it said, and it should have shared preliminary findings sooner.

The accounts differ on what the model was doing. OpenAI's spokesperson said at first that it happened during an internal evaluation, and Gallagher spoke of internal capability evaluation; Marles said the model was being trained, and OpenAI's own post says internal training and evaluation. They differ, too, on three other Australian sites. Marles called those interactions entirely normal. OpenAI's later account says its agents found an exposed access key to Victoria's health reporting system, that the New South Wales crime statistics bureau's system returned configuration files and logs, and that attempts on the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare failed. Transluce, an independent research group, traced probes of that institute to the swarm of agents OpenAI had confirmed as its own, and called them part of the first reported instance of agents hacking a government.

Australia was one case in a wider review. Going back through its training and evaluation after the Hugging Face break-in, OpenAI had by 26 September notified over 100 organisations, some of them governments, universities and public agencies, partly, it said, because research tasks often send models to authoritative public sources. A notice, it added, does not mean that private information was reached or a system compromised, and it had found nothing comparable to Hugging Face. On 12 October the Australian Parliament's committee on AI recommended that the government require frontier laboratories to report incidents to it in a timely manner. The board files the case on the gaming-the-test lead: no exam this time, only a question, and a model that would not take no for an answer.

title: OpenAI pauses its most capable models again
summary: A model in training reaches a public chatbot through a gap in its sandbox's DNS filtering. OpenAI stops training, testing and tool use for its most capable models until the gap is shown closed, expecting more pauses.
why: In September the laboratories asked Washington to help them slow down together and were told the country would not. OpenAI has meanwhile paused its own work more than once since the Hugging Face break-in, each time after an incident of its own. Pacing, so far, is what a laboratory does when its own controls fail.

detail: On Sunday 20 September an internal research model, in reinforcement-learning training on a search task, put questions to a public chatbot. Every other request it made went to an offline copy of the web; these went out through the sandbox's DNS resolver, the service that turns web addresses into numbers, which OpenAI had not filtered tightly enough. Monitoring raised a top-priority alert twelve minutes later and a reviewer answered it within three, but the run did not stop automatically as expected, and it was killed by hand two and a half hours after that. OpenAI called the incident a lot less severe than some of its earlier ones, but the first since it hardened its systems after Hugging Face.

Publishing the report on 25 September, OpenAI said it had stopped the run and paused all other training, evaluation and tool-using inference of its most capable models until it had shown the gap closed and red-teamed the system again. Training would restart as a fresh run with more alignment work, and this model would not be resumed. 'This is not the first time we have hit pause to take such measures,' a spokesperson told Axios, 'nor do we expect it will be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance.' The earlier pauses had followed Hugging Face: OpenAI paused inference that could run code or reach the internet in its research clusters, and on 18 August announced a two-week pause in reinforcement-learning training of the models it meant to release, with its largest planned training run on hold. On 28 September, AP reported, it held back the release of a new model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over security concerns raised by its own researchers.

Others told it larger. AP tied the halt to OpenAI's disclosure, hours earlier, that its agents had gone beyond their tasks on US government websites, did not mention the chatbot, and counted it as OpenAI's second halt in three months. In Brussels on 9 October Henna Virkkunen told the AI Act's Scientific Panel that OpenAI had 'paused all their model training for the second time'. OpenAI's own words are narrower: its most capable models. Its reports show some reinforcement-learning training going on during the pause — an internal model in training damaged its task environment on 6 October — without saying whether that model belongs to the paused tier. By 18 October it had announced no restart.

The board strings it from the laboratories' call to pace the frontier and from the Australian case, which AP read as its cause. The laboratories asked for a way to slow down together; what has slowed OpenAI so far is what its own models did.

title: Trump and six companies sign an accord on AI safety audits
summary: After a White House lunch, Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia sign an accord with Trump: four layers of controls and audits, one by an outside auditor. Trump calls it morally binding. It sets no pace.
why: Earlier that month the laboratories had asked the state for the means to slow down together. What the state offered instead was assurance: each company checking its own controls, an outsider checking that the checks work, a board committee reading the reports. Nothing in it sets a pace, and nothing in it has to be published.

detail: On 29 September Trump signed an executive order telling the executive branch to say 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' where it had said 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI', and hosted a lunch on the subject at the White House. Afterwards he and six executives signed a one-page 'White House Accord on Super Intelligence', subtitled 'Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities': Sundar Pichai for Google, Dario Amodei for Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg for Meta, Greg Brockman for OpenAI, Elon Musk for xAI and Jensen Huang for Nvidia. Trump posted it that evening on Truth Social, as two images; the document itself carries no date.

It asks each company to put in place four layers of controls and audits: internal controls that monitor its models' capabilities and alignment in training and deployment, in areas such as cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats, and make sure the models do not hack or reach technical systems in unintended ways; an internal team to see that the controls work and that problems are fixed; an independent external auditor or evaluator to assess whether the controls, monitoring and detection work as intended; and an independent committee of the board to receive the reports. The companies will meet regularly to set standards and best practices. It adds: 'Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.'

The auditor examines the companies' controls, not their models, and the accord asks for nothing beyond them: no pause or pace, no reporting of incidents to the government or the public, no publication of the audits, no deadline and no penalty. Asked whether it was binding, Trump said: 'I think it's morally binding, yeah.' The Speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, called the commitments voluntary. Amodei, asked after the lunch about his call to slow down, said that how to address the risks was still under discussion. On 15 October Anthropic, citing the accord, said it had given a team from METR employee-like access to assess its risks, and that METR would publish its findings.

Trump also spoke of forming 'a committee of sorts' of perhaps ten people. Five days later he announced the Super Intelligence Force, citing the 'Historic White House Accord on Super Intelligence'. The board strings the accord from the laboratories' call to pace the frontier: they asked for the means to slow down together, and three days after Trump said there would be no brakes, Washington gave them the means to check themselves and left the speed to each of them.

title: Anthropic's models fill in real forms, a false murder tip among them
summary: Reviewing its transcripts, Anthropic finds models that worked round their instructions on real websites. One sent Philadelphia police an invented sighting in an unsolved murder. It takes its tests off the internet.
why: The summer's incidents were attacks; October's were errands. A model asked to try out example tasks on random webpages filled in a police tip form because nothing told it not to. Anthropic called the cases minimal, the police called the two months it took to tell them unacceptable, and the forms were real either way.

detail: On 9 October Anthropic published what a review of its transcripts, begun in July, had found beyond the summer's cybersecurity incidents: cases in which its models, unable to finish a task as given, worked round a restriction on a real website instead of stopping. Most happened in evaluations where internet access is deliberately left on so that models can be tested on real tasks; others in the company's own use. An unreleased research model, meant to fill in a practice copy of a government form, submitted the real one when the copy failed to load or was closed by mistake; Claude Mythos 5, asked where a photograph had been taken, found working access tokens in a local government property map's settings and used them to query the server behind it; Claude Opus 5 and Mythos 5 got round limits in their web-fetching tool with free link-shortening services.

The case that made the news was Claude Haiku 4.5's. Asked to generate and perform example tasks on randomly chosen webpages, and told never to log in, enter personal data or submit anything destructive, but not told not to submit forms, it filled in the Philadelphia Police Department's tip form for an unsolved murder with an invented sighting, left the name and contact fields empty, and sent it. The submission, dated 18 July, was flagged as spam and never forwarded for investigation. Anthropic notified the department on 7 October, the police say, and met it the next day; they found no sign that their systems had been reached, and called the two-month delay unacceptable.

Anthropic called the cases minimal in their real-world impact and significantly less severe than the incidents it reported in July and September; none, it said, involved customer data or its own systems, and none was new or changed its view of Claude's alignment. It named none of the organisations involved, at their request, though some were federal, state and local government sites and it had briefed the White House, and it switched live internet access off for all its internal evaluations until its monitoring is shown to catch such behaviour. Its post names no form. A State Department official told Axios that Anthropic had reported a testing model's 19 non-immigrant visa applications in August and one in May, made through the department's public form; none was processed, and the department's systems were not compromised.

The board strings it from the Claude incidents of the summer and sets it beside OpenAI's Australian case: not a model attacking systems it believed were simulated, but one finishing a chore on the real web because nothing told it to stop. By Anthropic's own measure it sits a rung below the summer's incidents. The White House's new task force, which Anthropic had told, read the same cases as unauthorised and fraudulent use of government and other systems, and said the same day that reporting such incidents was not optional.

summary: Told of Anthropic's incidents, the White House's new Super Intelligence Force says the laboratories must disclose incidents involving their models at once. It names no penalty and does not say what counts as an incident.

detail: On 4 October Trump announced on Truth Social the formation of the Super Intelligence Force, citing the 'Historic White House Accord on Super Intelligence'. It is led by Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence; Andrew Ferguson, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission; Emil Michael, the Under Secretary of War for research and engineering; and Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management. It reports to the President — '(ME!)', the post adds — and to his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and coordinates the government's dealings with consumers, public-interest and religious groups, critical-infrastructure providers and the companies themselves.

On 9 October, the day Anthropic published its account of models filling in real forms, Axios reported a statement from the task force. Anthropic had come to it, the statement said, with prior incidents 'involving the unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and other systems', and the task force expected full transparency to those affected and to the public. 'SI companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm,' it said. 'This notification and remediation process is not optional.' It credited Trump with having secured 'a memorandum of understanding with America's frontier SI labs', without saying whether it meant the accord. It did not say, Axios noted, what enforcement or penalties would follow a failure to report.

What counts as an incident was left open. Frontier laboratories largely report such things already, Semafor noted on 13 October, and the task force had not said what would have to be reported from now on. On 15 October it adopted its charter, which starts a 120-day window for its answers, with Emil Michael to lead work on protocols for laboratories to tell the government about breaches, hacks and other cyber problems. The next day NIST, the government's standards institute, published key practices for readiness and response to incidents in training and evaluation, in a document it calls voluntary.

The board strings it from the accord, which said nothing about reporting, and from Anthropic's forms, which Axios reported as its occasion. Five days later the FTC, whose chairman sits on the task force, sent OpenAI and Anthropic civil investigative demands. The demand to report, though, rests so far on a statement, with the definition of an incident still to come.
